correctness.rationale: Adding a segment increases the area by its length times the width in the perpendicular direction, and widths add; this gives the absolute-determinant pair sum. Put t_n=τn^(−β), q_n=v t_n², and K=|sin(Θ_i−Θ_j)|−α. The canonical remainder kernel is exactly r²[(1+t_n ξ_i)(1+t_n ξ_j)K+αt_n²ξ_iξ_j]. The two terms are orthogonal by angular centering, and distinct pair kernels are uncorrelated by conditional degeneracy. Thus its one-pair variance is r⁴[(1+q_n)²(1/2−α²)+α²q_n²]; adding the first projection variance n(n−1)²α²r⁴q_n to the binomial(n,2) pair variances recovers the displayed variance, including β=0. Replacing the kernel by r²K has one-pair squared error r⁴[(2q_n+q_n²)(1/2−α²)+α²q_n²], giving the asserted L² bound. Direct integration gives cosine coefficient −4/[π(4m²−1)]; the sine/cosine coordinates each have variance 1/2 and are orthogonal, so the squared moduli in the finite-dimensional CLT are independent Exp(1) limits. Pair degeneracy and Fourier orthogonality give the stated uniform tail bound, and Parseval gives sum (4m²−1)^−2=(π²−8)/16. The unsquared sum telescopes to 1/2. Absolute summability gives L³ convergence by Minkowski, hence the strictly negative third cumulant; the upper support point is attained in the essential sense by requiring a finite exponential head to be small and controlling the independent nonnegative weighted exponential tail by its vanishing mean. The radial projection is an ordinary sample sum of scale n^(3/2−β); the angle-only remainder has scale n. At β=1/2 these independent finite-row terms converge jointly to independent nonzero limits by factorization of characteristic functions and Slutsky. These analytic checks establish the result; the uploaded geometry/Monte Carlo program was inspected but not run, and no finite simulation is offered as proof.

value.rationale: The degeneracy at constant generator length is natural in the isotropic planar model. The exact radial/angle variance split identifies the sensitivity of area to small independent radial noise, and determines both order and distribution on either side of a sharp threshold. The non-Gaussian critical convolution and calibratable finite-size variance add value beyond either classical fixed-law endpoint. The result is for the stated bounded-noise model and fixed exponents, not a uniform convergence rate or higher-dimensional theorem.
